card.hook: Picture a long wooden roof slanting across the river, with a chunky stone tower standing in the water beside it. That's Lucerne's best-known sight, and it all fits in one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Rathaussteg, the smaller footbridge downstream (west) of the Chapel Bridge. Face north-east and you'll see the long roofline and the octagonal Water Tower together, with the curly railings of your footbridge framing the scene.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bridge, the tower and a bit of river into one shot. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the tower or roof details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the roof up with a horizontal line so the bridge doesn't look tilted.
card.best_time: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the bridge. In the evening the softer light is kind to the timber, and night mode can help once it gets dark.
card.selfie_here: Try Wasserturmplatz, the square by the Water Tower end of the bridge, which is a popular spot for people to gather and take photos. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and check on the spot which way you need to turn so the bridge ends up over your shoulder. For a golden-hour silhouette, try the Seebrücke (the lake bridge near the station) while facing the Chapel Bridge.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the Rathaussteg and ask them to shoot back toward the Chapel Bridge and Water Tower, with you in the view.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep an eye on children near the river edges when taking photos. The bridge is a public footbridge, but the water tower is closed to the public, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Once you have the wide shot, walk onto the bridge and find a painted panel. Use the beams overhead to lead the eye straight to it.
card.good_to_know: The bridge was first built around 1365 as part of the town's defences, and it's described as the oldest wooden covered bridge in Europe. It's about 205 metres long, and the Wasserturm beside it is about 34.5 metres tall and was once a prison and a treasury. A fire on 18 August 1993 destroyed much of the bridge, and it reopened on 14 April 1994.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Rathaussteg, the smaller footbridge downstream (west) of the Chapel Bridge. Face north-east and you'll see the long roofline and the octagonal Water Tower together, with the curly railings of your footbridge framing the scene.

card.hook: A huge lion is dying in a cliff, and most people spend their first minute just staring at the water in front of it. That's the trick here: the still pond gives you a second lion, upside down.
card.stand_here: Head for the flat platform on the pond side of the park, straight across from the lion's head (the phone icon on the map sits right at the monument). Face the rock wall and you'll see the whole carving with the pond in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the lion and its reflection together. If you're too close, drop to 0.5x and keep the lion away from the edge of the screen, then try 2x or more for a close-up of the head and spear.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water line on the lower third, so the lion fills the top and its reflection fills the bottom.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or on an overcast day, when the light on the lion is nice and even. Early or quieter times of year also mean fewer people on the platform.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the pond edge in the park with the lion behind you (the exact bank isn't pinned down, so have a look on site). Use the front camera, try 0.5x so the carving fits over your shoulder, and tilt the phone a little so the pond is in the shot too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the viewing area on the far side of the pond, facing the rock face, while you stand at the pond edge with the lion behind you, so the whole lion and its reflection fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The park has had reconstruction work, so check the official site for any closures before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for the ripples to settle, then get the lion and its upside-down twin in one frame, with a little greenery sneaking in at the sides.
card.good_to_know: The Lion Monument was designed by Bertel Thorvaldsen and cut into the sandstone in 1820-21 by Lukas Ahorn. It remembers the Swiss Guards killed in Paris in 1792 during the French Revolution. The relief is about ten metres long and six metres high, and Mark Twain wrote about the lion mirrored among the water-lilies.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the flat platform on the pond side of the park, straight across from the lion's head (the phone icon on the map sits right at the monument). Face the rock wall and you'll see the whole carving with the pond in front.

selfie_spots.why: The sources describe the small pond in front of the lion as the park's most photogenic feature, so a shot taken there lets the monument sit in the background.

card.hook: Plot twist: the best photo at Lucerne's railway station doesn't have the station in it. Turn around and look at the lake instead, because the swans are doing most of the work.
card.stand_here: Stand on Schweizerhofquai, the lakeside promenade, on the lakefront about 300 m north of the station. Face out across the water to the lake, swans and mountains, with the hotel facades along the quay in view. The station is behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the lake, the hotel facades and the mountains together. Go 0.5x for more of the promenade, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the swans or to bring the mountains closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the water or the mountains, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, when the mountains show and the lake is calm enough to reflect them. Early morning is usually quieter on the quay.
card.selfie_here: Head to the paved plaza right outside the station and pose under the old arch, the Torbogen. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt the phone so the arch sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza at an angle to the arch while you stand by the arch, so both the arch and the glass station front appear behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is busy with buses and lake boats, so watch for traffic and people. Check locally that building work isn't affecting the square or the arch.
card.challenge: Get a swan and a mountain in the same shot, then see if you can catch the mountain reflected in the water too.
card.good_to_know: The first station here was wooden and opened on the lake edge in 1856. A bigger one with a cupola followed in 1896, then a fire on 5 February 1971 destroyed the frontage and concourse. The new station, with a concourse by Santiago Calatrava, opened exactly twenty years later, on 5 February 1991. The old arch survives out front, topped by the sculpture Zeitgeist by Richard Kissling.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Schweizerhofquai, the lakeside promenade, on the lakefront about 300 m north of the station. Face out across the water to the lake, swans and mountains, with the hotel facades along the quay in view. The station is behind you.

selfie_spots.why: The arch is the surviving remnant of the earlier station, so it gives a recognisable arrival backdrop right beside the modern building.

card.hook: Picture a whole building wearing 344 Swiss road signs like a giant, very bossy patchwork quilt. That's the road-transport hall at the Swiss Museum of Transport, and it's a gift for your camera roll.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Swiss Museum of Transport grounds, with the halls all around you. For the road-sign wall, walk back across the open space toward the edge of the site to fit it all in.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the big hall fronts and the road-sign wall, and 1x for the outdoor ship and submersible. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details like single road signs or the hull of the Rigi.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the hall edges straight, and if the sky is bright, tap the vehicle or sign and slide the brightness down a touch so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, since the outdoor displays are the stars. A bright but slightly cloudy day is perfect because it lights the signs and vessels evenly.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Verkehrshaus-Lido landing stage, the lakeside pier and park next to the museum, and use the front camera with the lake and mountains behind you. Nothing we found says the museum fits in that frame, so check the angle on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules and which areas you can enter may vary, and this is a ticketed museum, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the road sign that best matches your mood today, fill the frame with it, and make your travel buddy guess what it means.
card.good_to_know: The museum opened in July 1959 and is described as Switzerland's most popular museum. The submersible Mésoscaphe was built for the 1964 national exhibition, and the paddle steamer Rigi is the world's oldest surviving flush-deck side-wheeler. Inside, look out for a Moon rock and a satellite that came back to Earth.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, in the middle of the Swiss Museum of Transport grounds, with the halls all around you. For the road-sign wall, walk back across the open space toward the edge of the site to fit it all in.

card.hook: Picture the bridge at sunset, the old town's rooftops in front of you, and a long stretch of medieval-looking wall glowing in the distance. You get all that without climbing a single stair.
card.stand_here: Stand on Kapellbrücke and face north-west, where the Musegg Wall sits in the distance with Hotel Château Gütsch close by. Check the exact spot on the map before you set up.
card.zoom: Start at 2x or 3x to pull the wall and towers closer, then step back to 1x for a wider shot with the bridge and sky. Higher zooms depend on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the wall on one of the lower lines so the sky fills the frame, then tap the wall and slide a little darker to keep the sunset colours rich.
card.best_time: Go for sunset, when the light glows toward the wall. Wait until the sky actually colours before you take your main shots, then try night mode as the light fades (brace your phone on the bridge rail).
card.selfie_here: Try the grassy green area in front of the Zytturm clock face on the Musegg Wall, so the big clock and painted fresco are behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the tower fill the space over your shoulder. For another option, the north side between the Männliturm and Nölliturm has the towers rising behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The stairs up the towers can be quite steep, so take your time and wear comfy shoes.
card.challenge: Get the wall sitting on a lower gridline with a perfectly level horizon, and not one pigeon in the sky. Okay, the pigeon is optional.
card.good_to_know: The Musegg Wall (Museggmauer) is a stretch of town wall with towers, standing above Lucerne's old town. The towers are open to visitors only in the warmer part of the year, roughly April to November, so check the official site before you go. The outside views need no access at all.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Kapellbrücke and face north-west, where the Musegg Wall sits in the distance with Hotel Château Gütsch close by. Check the exact spot on the map before you set up.

card.hook: Most people walk into Spreuer Bridge without looking up, and that's a shame, because the roof is full of skeletons. Before you go in, grab the postcard view from outside.
card.stand_here: Stand in Mühlenplatz, at the mill-side (right bank) end of the bridge, and face west along the covered bridge. The red Mühlenturm tower sits in front of you, with the old town and city walls rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the bridge, the red tower and the old town all fit together. Only drop to 0.5x if you're tight against the buildings and the bridge won't fit. Save 2x or more for the painted panels or the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the bridge roof along one of the lower lines, and keep a strip of river along the bottom.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the timber and the red tower than harsh midday sun. Early in the day usually means fewer people on the bridge too.
card.selfie_here: Try Mühlenplatz at the bridge entrance. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the covered wooden bridge sits behind your shoulder. For a quieter, softer-light option, the stairs down to the riverside path just after the bridge have nice reflections, though the bridge will be a smaller part of the picture there.
card.ask_someone: If someone's nearby, the south bank of the Reuss near the Historisches Museum Luzern is where the bridge-with-city-walls view was shot, so it's a handy spot for them to stand while you pose at the bridge end.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public footbridge you can walk across, but check the official site before you go in case of any closures.
card.challenge: Take the wide shot first, then walk in and find a painted panel in the roof. Can you get one sharp photo of it without a stranger's head in the frame?
card.good_to_know: Spreuer Bridge is one of only two covered wooden bridges left in Lucerne. The name comes from the chaff (Spreu) people were once allowed to dump into the river from here. Inside the roof, a Dance of Death was painted between 1616 and 1637 under Kaspar Meglinger, and 45 of the original 67 panels survive.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Mühlenplatz, at the mill-side (right bank) end of the bridge, and face west along the covered bridge. The red Mühlenturm tower sits in front of you, with the old town and city walls rising behind it.

card.hook: Two green onion domes poke up over the Reuss like they're waving at the bridge. Once you spot them, you can't unsee them, and neither will your camera roll.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Kapellbrücke (Chapel Bridge), on the footpath side, and face back toward the church's twin towers across the river. The Reuss fills the bottom of your shot.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you catch the river and the bridge's flower boxes. Then tap 2x to bring the towers closer without chopping off the domes. Skip 0.5x here, because it makes the church look tiny and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the towers on one vertical line and let the water fill the lower third, then tap the church and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright so the domes stay green.
card.best_time: Early morning is a good bet: calmer bridge, soft light. Dusk works too if you use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing. For a sunrise scene with the Chapel Bridge and the church together, try the Reussbrücke.
card.selfie_here: Go to Jesuitenplatz, the open square in front of the church, and face away from the church so the detailed façade is behind you. Use the front camera, and if your phone has a 0.5x button, it helps squeeze more of the church in. The Chapel Bridge also works: stand between the posts and flower decorations with the church in view behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the Mill Bridge (Mühlenbrücke) and frame you with the church and the Reuss behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is an active place of worship. Inside, photos are only tolerated outside services, with no flash, so follow any posted signs and ask before photographing people.
card.challenge: Hide a flower box in one corner of the frame, but keep it small enough that the domes still win.
card.good_to_know: This is the first large Baroque church built in Switzerland north of the Alps. Work began in 1667 and it was consecrated in 1677, though the onion-topped towers weren't finished until 1893. It grew out of the Jesuit college, which the city council invited the Jesuits to set up in 1573. The Rathaussteg footbridge shows the north and east sides, but check it's still open.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Kapellbrücke (Chapel Bridge), on the footpath side, and face back toward the church's twin towers across the river. The Reuss fills the bottom of your shot.

card.hook: Forget hunting for the big viewpoint here. At the Glacier Garden of Lucerne, the best pictures are the small things right under your nose, so slow down and look closely.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Glacier Garden itself: the phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no extra walk to a separate viewpoint. Walk a little way in before you start shooting.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for most shots, then tap 0.5x to squeeze in a whole area. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put a strong line, like an edge or a path, along one of them to lead the eye in, then tap a detail and drag the brightness slider down a touch to keep the colours rich.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft, like a bright overcast day or a calm hour away from the middle of the day. You'll get gentler shadows and more even detail.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at arm's length, tap 0.5x to fit more of your surroundings in, and turn so the scene sits over your shoulder. Portrait mode can also work nicely if you're standing in front of the scene.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site for current opening information before you go.
card.challenge: Find a line that leads away from you, like a path or an edge, then put your bag in the foreground to show how big the scene feels.
card.good_to_know: The Glacier Garden is number 8 on the Lucerne map. That makes it a nice slower stop between the busier sights. Take a few wide shots of the whole setting, then a few close ones of interesting details, and wipe your phone's camera glass first because handling and outdoor air leave smudges.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Glacier Garden itself: the phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no extra walk to a separate viewpoint. Walk a little way in before you start shooting.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor can stand with the Glacier Garden itself behind them, or a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole garden in frame. The pages describe the mirror maze, the glacier potholes, and the observation tower, but none gives a framing position for the building. Two near-misses were not used: a Trip.com guide (https://www.trip.com/moments/theme/poi-glacier-garden-of-lucerne-18046351-attraction-993137/) suggests the water pool in front of the Lion Monument for reflection shots, but that frames the lion, not the garden; and the observation tower and outdoor terraces are described as giving views out over Lucerne, not as backdrops. No page states a selfie-stick or tripod rule for the Glacier Garden. The rules I found (Disney, Lauritzen Gardens) apply to other venues, and the no-climbing and no-touching rules on another Trip.com page apply to the Lion Monument. The Chasing Hippoz guide recommends a tripod for blue-hour shots in Lucerne generally, but that is advice, not a rule. No safety point was stated for this site.

card.hook: Picture a flat roof, 100 by 100 metres, hovering over the lake like a giant lid. That's the KKL, and the best way to get all of it in one photo is to stand back across the water.
card.stand_here: Stand in the lakeside Lido area, opposite the KKL across the water. Face west across the lake, and you'll see the KKL with the Kapellbrücke and the old town behind it.
card.zoom: At 1x the KKL looks small from over here, so zoom in to 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) until it fills about a third of the width. Keep the Kapellbrücke in view, then take one wider shot too. Save 0.5x for a close foreground like railings or plants.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour, and put the long roof on a gridline.
card.best_time: Pick a calm, clear morning or evening, when the light is softer and the lake may be smoother. The roof edge and the water look best then.
card.selfie_here: Try the Europaplatz plaza in front of the main entrance. Stand under the overhanging roof with the building at your back, use the front camera and hold it a bit low so the roof fits in. If the KKL terrace is open, face the lake from just under the roof and the building sits behind you. Both spots are worth a quick check when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Chapel Bridge over the Reuss to shoot back toward the KKL with you in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The KKL terrace and interior can be closed during events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the roofline sitting on a gridline, a strip of lake along the bottom, and the Kapellbrücke peeking in, all in one shot.
card.good_to_know: French architect Jean Nouvel designed the KKL. The concert hall opened on 18 August 1998, and the whole complex was inaugurated in March 2000. Inside you'll find a concert hall, an art museum, conference rooms and restaurants. It's also the main home of the Lucerne Festival.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the lakeside Lido area, opposite the KKL across the water. Face west across the lake, and you'll see the KKL with the Kapellbrücke and the old town behind it.

card.hook: This calm, formal building with the straight stone front looks like a bank because it used to be one. That's good news for you: it makes a tidy, symmetrical photo.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Rosengart Collection Museum. Face the front of the building and take in the whole façade before you do anything else.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole front. If you can't step back far enough, drop to 0.5x and hold the phone level so the edges don't stretch. Then try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the doorway and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the edges of the façade up with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft daylight, like morning or late afternoon, usually looks best on a façade like this. If the sky is bright, tap the stonework and make the picture a little darker so the building keeps its detail.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and step back a little, with the building behind you. If you're close, try 0.5x so you can squeeze the whole front in over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the museum, personal photos with a smartphone are allowed, but flash and selfie sticks are not. Check the official site before you go for visiting details.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then one close-up of the entrance or the stonework. Can you make both look as straight as a bank vault door?
card.good_to_know: The building is a neoclassical former bank, built in 1923-1924 by Zurich architect Hermann Herter, and it once belonged to the Swiss National Bank. The Rosengart family bought it, and architect Roger Diener converted it. It opened as a museum on 26 March 2002, and inside you'll find Picasso on the ground floor and Klee in the basement.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Rosengart Collection Museum. Face the front of the building and take in the whole façade before you do anything else.

rules.rule: Private photography for personal use is allowed inside with a smartphone or compact camera, but flash photography, tripods and selfie sticks are barred. Pre-arranged professional shoots need advance approval.

The official site is the more reliable source here.

card.hook: Look up from the old wooden bridge and there's a white fairy-tale castle sitting above the dark forest, like someone forgot to tell it Lucerne is a real city. It's actually a hotel, and it's the best layered photo in town.
card.stand_here: Stand on Spreuerbrücke, where the château is about 514 m to the west in a straight line, with a climb up the hill. Face up the Reuss toward the hill and you'll see it above the forest, with the Old Town rooftops in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the rooftops, trees and hill all fit. Then try zoom 2x to bring the château closer and squeeze the forest and building together.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white façade, then slide the brightness down a little so the castle keeps its detail against the dark trees.
card.best_time: Morning to early afternoon is likely to be kindest, because the sun should be behind you and light up the château's front. Later in the day you'll be shooting toward the sun, so expect a darker, backlit castle.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the small terrace beside the hotel entrance, where the Grand Tour of Switzerland photo frame stands, or the hotel terrace itself. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the city and lake over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The château is a private hotel complex, and the funicular and terrace may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go. Check that the funicular is running too.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and catch all three layers in one shot: rooftops at the bottom, dark trees in the middle, and the white château on an upper intersection.
card.good_to_know: The château went up in 1888 in a romantic, castle-like style. In 1901 it got the look it has now, modelled on Neuschwanstein in Bavaria. It reopened as a hotel in 2014 after a long closure and has 27 rooms.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Spreuerbrücke, where the château is about 514 m to the west in a straight line, with a climb up the hill. Face up the Reuss toward the hill and you'll see it above the forest, with the Old Town rooftops in front.

card.hook: Step inside and suddenly you're standing in the middle of a freezing February in 1871, with thousands of tired soldiers all around you. Your camera roll is about to look very dramatic.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map sits right at the subject, so once you reach the Bourbaki Panorama building in Lucerne you're already there. Inside, head for the centre of the circular painting, where the scene wraps around you in every direction.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the big sweep of the painting plus the real props in front of it. Then use 1x for natural-looking views, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for faces, horses and the meeting of the two generals.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the rail tracks and straight roads so they lead the eye off into the distance.
card.best_time: We don't have opening times, so check the official site before you go. The light inside is probably fairly steady, so the time of day matters less than picking a quiet moment. Early morning is suggested if you want fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Go to the ground-level foreground display inside the rotunda, among the life-sized figures and the railway box car, and turn so the painting is behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone offers it) and hold it a little low so the props and the painting both squeeze in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: On Löwenplatz outside the entrance, ask a passer-by to stand back far enough to fit the whole building and its round top in the frame, while you stand in front of the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is typically not allowed, to protect the artwork, so turn it off and check the signs or ask staff when you arrive.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot and one close-up of a single face, then see which one makes your friends say 'wait, is that real?'
card.good_to_know: The painting is 115 metres around and shows French soldiers crossing into neutral Switzerland in February 1871, while locals and Red Cross helpers look after the wounded. Swiss painter Édouard Castres, who travelled with the army as a medical volunteer, led the work with ten other artists. It was first shown in Geneva in 1881 and has been in Lucerne since 1889. It was cut down twice, so it's now 9.8 metres tall.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map sits right at the subject, so once you reach the Bourbaki Panorama building in Lucerne you're already there. Inside, head for the centre of the circular painting, where the scene wraps around you in every direction.

card.hook: Picture a plain, cube-shaped manor house on a small green mound, with Lake Lucerne right beside the path leading up to it. It's a simple scene, and the walk up gives you a real sense of arrival.
card.stand_here: Stand on Richard-Wagner-Weg, the lakeside path that leads up to the museum. The villa is just ahead of you to the north, with the lake beside the path, so face straight up the path.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the villa along the path. Try 0.5x if you want more lake and grounds, but keep the house away from the edges of the frame so the corners don't stretch. For the steps and entrance, try 2x if your phone has it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the path up with one of the lower grid lines so it leads the eye straight to the house.
card.best_time: Pick a bright, dry day, so the lake and the mountains behind the park are clear. Early or late in the day the light is softer and the path is usually quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the lawn at the museum grounds on the lake shore, where the park runs down to the water below the villa. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the lake and mountains fill in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the forecourt in front of the villa, beside the Sommercafé, and frame you with the villa and the lake and mountains behind.
card.rules_and_safety: If you take photos inside the museum, skip the flash. Rules can change, so look for signs at specific exhibits or ask staff.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole villa, then one close-up of the entrance steps, and see which one you like better.
card.good_to_know: The building dates from the 15th century and took its present form in 1623. Wagner lived here from 1866 to 1872 and finished Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg and Siegfried in the house. His Siegfried Idyll was first played on the stairs on Christmas morning 1870, and the city turned the villa into a museum in 1933.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Richard-Wagner-Weg, the lakeside path that leads up to the museum. The villa is just ahead of you to the north, with the lake beside the path, so face straight up the path.

card.hook: Here's a little twist: the best photo of Lucerne's famous twin-tower church isn't taken at the church. You take it from a creaky old wooden bridge, with the towers poking up behind the roof beams.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Kapellbrücke, the covered wooden bridge over the Reuss, and face north-east. The church (the Hofkirche) is about 618 m north-east of this stand-here point, so the two towers rise behind the bridge.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the bridge and both towers fit. If the towers look tiny, try 2x up to 5x (it depends on your phone), but keep some of the bridge in the shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the towers on an upper line, and let the bridge roof and river fill the bottom of the picture.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late afternoon light usually suits the towers and the wooden bridge.
card.selfie_here: Try the churchyard terrace edges, where you can have the church behind you and the view down toward the lake. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the towers fit over your shoulder. The garden beside the church is a quiet, photogenic backup with fewer tourists.
card.ask_someone: Stand a few steps down the front staircase from the facade and ask your helper to shoot from a few steps farther out, so the church fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the church, no flash and keep it quiet. Don't step onto the roped-off altar area, and respect anyone praying or attending Mass.
card.challenge: Can you catch both towers poking out above the bridge roof without the beams chopping them off? Bonus points if you keep the phone dead level.
card.good_to_know: The church was built in parts between 1633 and 1639, after a fire in 1633 destroyed the earlier building. A religious house has stood on this site since the 8th century. It became the parish church in 1874, which is why it's still in everyday use.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Kapellbrücke, the covered wooden bridge over the Reuss, and face north-east. The church (the Hofkirche) is about 618 m north-east of this stand-here point, so the two towers rise behind the bridge.
